title: Reading assembly without panic
lead: Lectures 6–8: program representations, x86-64 instructions, stack frames, and arrays.
example:
Today’s path

C → assembly → machine code
Read operands and trace values
Follow a call and its stack frame
Connect arrays to byte addresses
caption: Goal: explain what a short snippet does, one instruction at a time.
notes: Suggested 50-minute pacing: representation and floating point 6 min; assembly syntax and tracing 21 min; calls and stack 12 min; arrays and practice 11 min. Source: lectures 6–8.

title: Floating point is approximate
lead:
A float stores a finite set of values. The gaps grow as the magnitude grows.

An intermediate result can round before the next operation, so rearranging arithmetic may change the answer.
example:
With finite precision:

(a + b) + c  may differ from
a + (b + c)

Try: a = 3.14, b = 1e10, c = -1e10

The large addition can lose 3.14.
caption: Do not use algebraic rearrangement as a guaranteed floating point equivalence.
notes: Lecture 6 shows float rounding with 3.14, 1e10, and -1e10. Exact output depends on type and evaluation environment. This slide teaches the principle without promising a platform-independent numeric result.

title: ALU, FPU, and instructions
lead:
The ALU handles integer arithmetic and logic. The FPU handles floating point work.

Machine instructions choose operations and operands. Assembly gives those instructions readable names.
example:
C:            a = a + 8;
Assembly:     addl $8, -4(%rbp)
Machine code: instruction bytes
Hardware:     decode, then execute
caption: The example assembly is one possible unoptimized x86-64 translation, not a required compiler output.
notes: Use lecture 6's C/addl/objdump progression. Compilers may choose registers or optimize the entire expression away, so avoid teaching a single assembly listing as universal.

title: One line of AT&T assembly
lead:
Read the source first, then the destination. The destination changes.

The suffix says how much data is used: b = 1 byte, w = 2, l = 4, q = 8.
example:
movq $5, %rax

movq   move 8 bytes
$5     literal value 5
%rax   destination register

Afterward: %rax = 5
caption: AT&T syntax is the format used in these lectures and by GCC’s default assembly output.
notes: Ask students to point to the value that changes. Contrast Intel syntax only if a student asks: its operand order is reversed. Source: lectures 6 and 7.

title: Three kinds of operands
lead:
A dollar sign means the value itself. A percent sign names a register. Parentheses mean memory at an address.

These are different even when the same digits appear.
example:
$8          value 8
%rax        value inside rax
(%rax)      memory at address in rax
8(%rax)     memory at address rax + 8

movq $8, %rax   → rax becomes 8
movq (%rax), %rbx → load from address 8
caption: The last line only makes sense if address 8 is readable; it illustrates syntax, not a safe program.
notes: Use an analogy: a register holds a street address; parentheses mean visit that street address. Distinguish $8 from 8(%rax) carefully. In real user programs address 8 is normally invalid; replace with a valid pointer for a live demo.

title: Trace two instructions
lead:
Start with %rax = 100 and %rbx = 7.

What is in each register after these lines?

Which register changed on each line?
caption: Read each line left to right: source, then destination.
notes: Pause before showing the answer. Have students narrate the two changes aloud. Source operands are read; the destination receives the result.

title: Trace answer
lead:
The first line copies 7 into %rax. The second adds 3 to that copy.

%rbx never changes.
example:
Initially       rax = 100   rbx = 7
movq %rbx,%rax  rax =   7   rbx = 7
addq $3,%rax   rax =  10   rbx = 7
caption: A move copies a value; it does not erase the source.
notes: Common confusion: students may think 'move' transfers and clears rbx. Emphasize that it copies. Then ask what subq $2, %rax would do: rax becomes 8.

title: Registers have different widths
lead:
%rax is 64 bits. %eax names its low 32 bits; %ax names the low 16; %al names the low 8.

Writing %eax zeroes the upper 32 bits of %rax. Reading %eax does not change %rax.
example:
movq $-1, %rax
movl $1, %eax

Now %rax = 0x0000000000000001

movq  ↔  %rax  ↔  8 bytes
movl  ↔  %eax  ↔  4 bytes
caption: This zero-extension rule applies to 32-bit register destinations in x86-64.
notes: Lecture 7 discusses register aliases and movl. Be precise: writing a 32-bit register zeroes the upper 32 bits; a movl from %eax into memory does not clear the upper half of %rax. Do not generalize this rule to 8- or 16-bit writes.

title: Array indexing is byte arithmetic
lead:
Memory addresses count bytes. For an int array, element i begins 4i bytes after the start when int is 4 bytes.

The addressing form combines base + index × scale + displacement.
caption: The scale is the size of an element in bytes; 8 adds two more int positions here.
notes: Assume sizeof(int)==4 for this example; the C standard does not require int to be 4 bytes on every platform. Draw boxes at addresses base, base+4, base+8, base+12. Source: lectures 6–8.

title: Address versus value
lead:
leaq computes an address and places that number in a register.

movq with a memory source reads the value stored at an address.
example:
Assume rax = 1000, memory[1008] = 42

leaq 8(%rax), %rbx  → rbx = 1008
movq 8(%rax), %rcx  → rcx = 42
caption: lea does not dereference memory, even though its source looks like a memory operand.
notes: Ask: which instruction could compute &a[2], and which could load a[2]? Clarify that movq reads eight bytes here; the made-up memory value 42 is an eight-byte value for this trace. Source: lecture 8 sieve assembly and lecture 7 RIP-relative example.

title: A branch is an if statement
lead:
cmpq compares two operands and sets condition flags. A conditional jump reads those flags.

ja means unsigned “jump if above.” The target is a label elsewhere in the code.
example:
C: if (n > 1) return n;

cmpq $1, %rdi
ja   .Lbig
movl $1, %eax
ret
.Lbig:
movq %rdi, %rax
ret
caption: Here %rdi is an unsigned 64-bit n; %rax carries the return value.
notes: For AT&T cmpq $1, %rdi, flags describe rdi minus 1. ja is true for unsigned rdi > 1. This matches lecture 7's unsigned sequence example. Distinguish signed jg from unsigned ja when asked. In a real compiled function there may be setup/cleanup instructions.

title: Trace the branch
lead:
Use the previous snippet. Predict the return value for n = 0, 1, and 4.

For each input, decide whether ja jumps before following any other line.
example:
n = 0  → ja? ___  return ___
n = 1  → ja? ___  return ___
n = 4  → ja? ___  return ___

Hint: “above 1” is strict, not ≥ 1.
caption: Check your answer by following only the instructions on the chosen path.
notes: Give partners time to trace. Ask one student why n=1 does not jump. The next slide moves to calls and stack frames.

title: Function calls use conventions
lead:
For ordinary integer or pointer arguments on the x86-64 System V ABI, the first arguments use %rdi, %rsi, %rdx, %rcx, %r8, %r9.

The return value usually arrives in %rax.
caption: This convention applies to the Linux x86-64 examples in the lectures; floating point arguments use different registers.
notes: Make clear this is an ABI convention, not an inherent meaning of the registers. The call instruction also saves a return address. Source: lectures 6 and 7.

title: The stack keeps each call’s state
lead:
The stack grows toward lower addresses. %rsp points at its current top.

A function may save the old %rbp, set a new frame base, and subtract from %rsp to reserve space for local data.
example:
pushq %rbp        save old frame
movq %rsp, %rbp   set frame base
subq $16, %rsp   reserve 16 bytes
...
leave             restore old frame
ret               return to caller
caption: These are common unoptimized patterns, not instructions every function must contain.
notes: Lecture 8 gives this prologue and epilogue. Correct mental model: pushq decrements rsp by 8 then writes; popq reads then increments rsp by 8. call pushes the return address, ret pops it. Optimized code may omit rbp or use different frame layouts.

title: A stack frame in addresses
lead:
Suppose %rsp is 0x1000 just after call has placed the return address on the stack.

Follow the three setup instructions. Which address holds the saved %rbp? Where does the new frame begin?
example:
Start             rsp = 0x1000
pushq %rbp        rsp = 0x0ff8
movq %rsp,%rbp    rbp = 0x0ff8
subq $16,%rsp     rsp = 0x0fe8

Saved rbp: [0x0ff8]
Return address: [0x1000]
caption: Local stack space is at addresses below the new %rbp.
notes: Walk down by eight bytes for pushq, then by sixteen for local space. The address notation here is conceptual, not a literal disassembly. The return address was pushed by call before the stated starting point.

title: Arrays and sizeof
lead:
An array stores elements in consecutive memory. In its own scope, sizeof array measures its total bytes.

A function parameter written as int a[] is treated as a pointer, so sizeof a there measures the pointer.
caption: For a VLA, sizeof can be evaluated at run time. In a parameter, it still describes a pointer.
notes: Lecture 8 covers known-size arrays, VLAs, and array parameters. Avoid claiming sizeof(pointer) always equals 8: that is platform dependent. A parameter written int a[10] is also adjusted to a pointer; the 10 does not enforce array length for a function argument.

title: Variable length arrays and lifetime
lead:
A VLA gets its length at run time. Its elements need explicit initialization.

Local array storage ends when its scope ends, so returning a pointer to that array leaves a dangling pointer.
caption: For data that must survive a function return, use an appropriate allocation and ownership plan.
notes: Source: lecture 8. The exact maximum safe VLA size depends on available stack space. C language support for VLAs depends on the chosen C version and compiler; use course tooling for live examples. A local array's storage duration, rather than whether its bytes are immediately overwritten, determines pointer validity.

title: One final trace
lead:
Assume int is 4 bytes, %rax holds &a[0], and %rcx = 2.

What address does leaq compute? What value does movl read?
caption: Sketch four boxes, each four bytes wide, before calculating.
notes: Expected: rdx = 0x2008 and eax = 30. The address is base + 2*4. Have students explain why leaq does not put 30 in rdx.

title: Trace answer and checklist
lead:
leaq computes 0x2000 + 2×4 = 0x2008. movl reads the 4-byte int at that address: 30.

When assembly feels dense, mark the operand type, track the changed register, then follow the next instruction.
example:
%rdx = 0x2008   address of a[2]
%eax = 30       value of a[2]

$        literal
%        register
(...)    memory
q/l      8/4 bytes
caption: Read the relevant C beside the assembly, then verify one step at a time.
notes: Close by pointing students to lectures 6–8 for the larger examples. Suggest compiling a very small C function with gcc -O0 -S and finding its arguments, arithmetic, and return value; compiler output may vary.
